_comment: EVERY gameplay tunable in TROPHIC. Guardrail G11 / INV-4: no gameplay constant may be a literal in code — all read from this file. Retuning balance touches this file only (INV-3). Sources are cited per group; anything sourced 'build-doc addition' is explicitly tunable there.
_singleSource: No number in this file may also be written somewhere else in data/. Numbers the bible states FOR A NAMED MOVE (powers 40/70/50/60, Singe/Douse 20%, Regrow 30%, Trample +25, Terrify 2 turns) are CONTENT and live only in data/moves.json; magnitudes the bible names without numbering live only here, referenced from moves.json by `magnitudeKey`. tests/unit/transcription.test.ts gates both directions.

types._source: bible §1 — multiplier VALUES only; the chart SHAPE is content and lives in data/moves.json.

age._source: bible §2 age multiplier; bible §4 lifespan on catch; build-doc §3 L9 / §7.4 metamorphic jump.
age._multiplier: HALVED from J 0.75 / A 1.0 / E 1.15 on Hank's ruling (T-10): 'reduce the age buff/nerf to have half the effect it currently does'. Half the DEVIATION FROM NEUTRAL, not half the value — A is neutral so it does not move; J = 1.0 - (1.0-0.75)/2 = 0.875; E = 1.0 + (1.15-1.0)/2 = 1.075. metamorphicJump is deliberately NOT halved: build-doc §7.4 makes it a separate once-only term carried by metamorphic lines, not the J/A/E multiplier, and the ruling named only the age buff/nerf. retirement.heirLevelFactor stays 0.5 for the same reason — he was explicit. WHAT IT BOUGHT, measured on the shipped content with the two complaints the ruling names, at 64 seeds per cell (instrument: both sides on core/battle.ts's own argmax, no traits, opponents weighted by the shipped Route 1 populations and the real act-1 level band): a level-5 JUVENILE starter's Route 1 loss rate fell 77.6% -> 66.2% while the ADULT's rose 11.7% -> 13.3%, closing the J/A gap 65.9 pp -> 53.0 pp; and the heir's power drop at retirement fell 2.12x -> 1.70x, its age term 1.76x -> 1.41x (metamorphic) and 1.53x -> 1.23x (non-metamorphic, which is the log-halving read literally: 48.2% of the old term). The heir's win rate against the act-4 wild ladder rose from 0.3-4.2% to 10.2-17.3%, which is the never-cut Legacy beat. THE ROUTE 1 FIGURES ABOVE ARE THE AGE CHANGE ALONE. The T-11 Producer re-spend landed after them and moved Route 1 again in the other direction — see data/species.json _bandArithmetic, which carries those numbers.

stats._source: bible §2 — effective stat = Base × AgeMult × (1 + 0.02 × Level) + trait modifiers; traits are flat ±10%.

traits._source: bible §2 — 'Traits: flat ±10% modifiers with names ("Thick Pelt: +10% Defense"). 1 per wild creature, +1 slot via inheritance, Elders roll rare traits.' The MAGNITUDE is stats.traitModPct (never repeated per trait); the pool below carries only name/stat/direction/rarity. Rare traits are the Elder-only pool and are always beneficial — that is what makes an Elder roll worth having. Names other than 'Thick Pelt' (bible-verbatim) and 'Silk-Spun' are coined, and are in scope for the G15 IP sweep. The pool is a 5×3 lattice — per stat, a common up, a common down and a rare up — so a name has to read as its column: 'Bright Eye' is the positive of 'Dulled Sense', 'Broad Jaw' the positive of 'Soft Bite'. Those two names are IP renames: the ids `keen-eye` and `strong-jaw` DID NOT MOVE and never render, but the display names 'Keen Eye' and 'Strong Jaw' were exact matches for Pokémon Abilities #51 and #173.

damage._source: build-doc §7.4 damage roll; crit is driven by Instinct (bible §2) and is a build-doc-addition tunable.

status._source: build-doc §7.4 — Burn 6%/turn chip; Toxin 4% ramping +2%/turn; Soak −30% Speed; Daze 25% skip. One status at a time, newest wins. NOTE: the light-type-move apply chance is NOT here — bible §3 states it per move ('Singe (40, 20% Burn)'), so it is content and lives once, in data/moves.json.

moves._source: bible §3 — 'Each creature has exactly 4 move slots: 2 type moves + 1 role move + 1 utility, unlocked at levels 1/5/10/15'; build-doc §7.1 repeats the 1/5/10/15 in movePool slot order. Keyed by the movePool slot names so core/battle.ts can answer 'which moves does a level-7 creature know' from data alone (G11 / INV-4).

moveEffects._source: Magnitudes bible §3 names without numbering ('+Defense', '+evasion'). Moves reference these by magnitudeKey so no magnitude is a literal in code or duplicated in moves.json.

battle._source: bible §3 utility move Burrow/Roost — 'skip turn, +evasion'; build-doc §7.4 statuses + status.persistUntilCured.
battle._why: evadeTurns 1 = the evasion covers the turn the user spent skipping and no longer. (The evade also resolves BEFORE the opponent's attack — core/battle.ts `movePriority` — because an evade applied after the hit it is meant to duck mitigates nothing, which made the move strictly dominated for every creature slower than its opponent.) Any larger duration makes a 0-power utility move strictly better than attacking, which would break the §10.5 round-robin band. statusWearOffTurns is consulted ONLY when status.persistUntilCured is false: with the shipped `true` a status never wears off on its own (build-doc §7.4 names no expiry), so the number is inert at ship — it exists so that flipping the advertised flag in the balance harness actually changes behaviour instead of doing nothing.

catch._source: build-doc §7.4 catch formula (build-doc addition, tunable), as amended under Hank's authorisation to give the bait term an Instinct factor: p = baseCatch(age) × snareTier × (baitMult × instinctBait) × (2 − hpFrac)/2 × lureMult, clamped.
catch._instinctBait: bible §2 gives Instinct three jobs — 'crit chance, bait success, sign-reading quality' — and until this amendment core/battle.ts read it for crit alone, which made Instinct the strongest and NEGATIVE predictor of round-robin win rate (r = -0.582). The bait term now scales with the CATCHING creature's Instinct: instinctBait = 1 + instinctBaitSlope × (insShare − instinctBaitPivot), where insShare = ins / (hp+atk+def+spd+ins) over that creature's EFFECTIVE stats. The SHARE, not the raw stat, is what a point of Instinct actually costs: every non-Ancient line spends exactly 300 base points (data/species.json _statRule), and because the age, level, metamorphic and Beast multipliers are common to all five stats they cancel out of the ratio — so the term reads ALLOCATION and cannot become a level-scaled global catch buff. In-battle stat mods are deliberately NOT read (raising your own Defense with Bristle — move id `harden` — would otherwise lower your catch odds). instinctBaitPivot is the roster's MEDIAN Instinct allocation, 45/300 = 0.15, so a median-Instinct catcher is unchanged from the pre-amendment formula; measured over the 24 non-Ancient lines the term spans ×0.846 (base ins 30) to ×1.257 (base ins 70) with a roster mean of ×1.010. Positive over the whole mathematically possible share range [0,1] — 1 + 3×(0−0.15) = 0.55 — so the term never flips the sign of a probability; the .02–.95 clamp still binds at both ends.

medicine._source: bible §11 — 'Medicines — salve (field heal), tonic (status cure), inn rest (full heal, 2 ticks).' The bible names the effects without numbering them, so the magnitudes are build-doc-addition tunables. Item ids live here too so BattleAction {kind:"item", itemId} resolves without a literal in code (G11). Inn tick cost is clock.innTicks.

xp._source: build-doc §7.4 (build-doc addition, tunable): xpGain = 12 + 4×enemyLevel × ageBonus(E:1.3); xpToNext(l) = 15 × l^1.4; cap 40.

ecosim._source: build-doc §7.3 numbered population step. presence multipliers per bible §4 Ancients.
ecosim._demand: demand[s] = count[s] × demandPerIndividual[role of s] (role read at webRoleAgeClass). Per-ROLE because the pyramid is per-role: one global figure cannot make an Apex starve when its prey crash without starving every Mesopredator at the shipped state. A role whose value is 0 has NO live diet at all (bible §5: Producers photosynthesise, Scavengers 'eat nothing live', Ancients 'eat nothing') — for those the sim uses noDietFoodFactor and skips the §7.3 step-2 starvation check entirely, instead of dividing by zero or starving them to extinction. Values are calibrated against the shipped node counts so that (a) nothing starves at the shipped state and (b) any Apex whose derived prey pool falls to 10% crosses starveThreshold — build-doc §10.2 `cascade_emerges`. Both directions are gated by tests/unit/transcription.test.ts.
ecosim._starveTermination: build-doc §7.3 steps 2 and 4 leave one gap between them: with `deaths = count × starveRate` alone, a starving population of 3 goes 2.1 → 1.47 → 1.03 → 0.72 and, under stochastic rounding, can sit at 1 individual indefinitely — so a crash never RESOLVES and `apex count → 0` (§10.2 `cascade_emerges`) is not a law, only a likelihood. These two keys make starvation terminal: a starving population loses at least one individual per season and does not breed while starving. Both are general rules over every species at every node (no species is named anywhere — G6); neither can fire at the shipped node states, where the lowest food ratio is 0.67 against a starveThreshold of 0.4.
ecosim._presenceEffects: bible §4 states what each Ancient's presence does — Vellsire 'buffs all breeding rates in adjacent nodes (keystone)', Kilnback 'keeps the steppe vents warm (Fire spawns active)', Undermere 'steadies the marsh water table (Water breeding)'. The MAGNITUDES are keystoneBreedMult / ventWarmthBreedMult / waterTableBreedFloor above, but nothing said which type an effect acts on or whether it multiplies or floors — so both had to be decided in core/ecosim.ts, where `if (effect === "waterTable")` was a bare code literal (G11) that, because data/species.json carries exactly ONE line per effect name, was in practice `if (this is Undermere)` (G6). Both halves now live here: `mode` selects the SHAPE of the effect from a structural vocabulary (PRESENCE_MODES) that any number of Ancients could share, `type` names what it acts on, and `magnitudeKey` points at the number above rather than repeating it (one number, one home). Adding a fourth Ancient with an existing shape is a data edit (INV-1), not a code edit.

cascade._source: build-doc §10.2 states the `cascade_emerges` property in numbers — 'forcing its primary prey to <10% for 2 consecutive seasons yields apex count →0 and mesopredator count strictly rising within 4 seasons'. They are thresholds of the CLAIM, not of the sim, so they live here rather than as literals in tests/property/ecosim.test.ts. `mesoReleaseSeasons` is the window the release clause is measured over, counted from the season the apex reaches 0.
cascade._coverage: The two coverage floors below are the property test's own thresholds, kept out of the test body for the same reason as the four above: they are claims about the shipped content, and a reviewer must be able to see what strength was claimed without reading a test. `mesoSurvivesForcingMinFraction` is the fraction of seeds in which a mesopredator whose forced target is at least one individual is still alive when the apex reaches 0 (measured at r4: 0.66). `releaseCoverageMinFraction` is the fraction of generated cascades in which anything survived to be released (measured: ~0.4).

clock._source: build-doc §3 L8, as amended under Hank's authorisation — 52-tick YEAR meter (one tick reads as a week), 13 ticks per season, four seasons. travel 1 / foray 1 / inn 2 / battle 0.5. A gym victory no longer ends a year. NOTE the meter is the YEAR's, not the season's: docs once said '16-tick season meter' and that phrase put a wrong number into a work ticket. RETUNING: these are expected to move again after playtesting. ticksPerYear must stay ticksPerSeason x seasonOrder.length and every cost must be an exact multiple of 1/subTicksPerTick — core/schemas.ts refuses to boot otherwise, so a bad retune fails loudly at startup instead of silently dropping time.
clock._yearsTotal: NOT A CAP. The calendar is unbounded — year may be 9 or 40 and nothing stops it. yearsTotal is the EXPECTED year count under normal pacing: six acts at roughly a year each, which is what the HUD quotes, what the balance harness drives by default, and what the six-year property trajectories measure. Story progression is the ACT model's (see `acts`), and no code may read this key to decide whether the run is over.

acts._source: THE SECOND CLOCK (Hank's ruling: 'the game should progress based on the player going through the gyms and side events, not based on year progression. Simply switch out the time check points for event check points.'). Acts are driven by badges and quest flags and NEVER by time; the calendar (see `clock`) is driven by ticks and never by acts. The rows below transcribe content-bible §6 (the six towns and their one route each, in order) and §7 (the six leaders, in order) — no town, route or leader is invented here (G2). The flag names are the ones data/dialogue.json already reads: `gym.<id>.beaten`, `story.opening.done`, `story.greaves.beaten`.
acts._act0: Act 0 is the prologue: a save that has not finished Maren's opening chain. It is a real, reachable state — a new save starts there — and it opens Hearthollow alone, which is bible §6's 'Warden Maren's field station: starter choice, bait-crafting intro, tutorial forage'. Act 1 opens when `story.opening.done` is set, at zero badges.
acts._noCap: `last` is the last act the region HAS, not a deadline. Nothing fails, expires or ends when the calendar passes it, and a player may sit in act 1 for twenty years.

regionalEvents._source: bible §9's four regional events, as SEASON-LONG WINDOWS. Hank, 2026-08-25: 'events like that last for a whole season and not just for one in-game day.' A window opens on a season boundary, stays open for clock.ticksPerSeason ticks and closes at the next boundary — core/regional-events.ts. The Annual Festival is the year's final season (bible §9 amended: it no longer CLOSES the year, it spans the season the meter fills in); the Great Migration is a migrant's seasonalWindow (data/species.json, already a season by construction); a Cullbrand raid's window is the season its ACT was entered in; a Bloom Year is a node whose flora clears the fraction below at a season boundary.
regionalEvents._bloomFraction: bible §9 'a route whose producers thrive gets bonus spawns' names no number. Expressed as a FRACTION of ecosim.floraMax rather than an absolute so it cannot become a second copy of that ceiling (this file's _singleSource rule). The BONUS-SPAWN half of §9's sentence is RULED CLOSED, not unruled (T-7): it is never built and never owed, because weighting an encounter here would be a second spawn table and G3 gives that job to core/foodweb.ts alone. The bible was amended to match. The window ships; the multiplier does not, and nobody should add one.
regionalEvents._flagNames: A window publishes itself as the quest flag `<windowFlagPrefix><windowId><windowFlagSuffix>`. The names are chosen so the festival's flag is `event.festival.open` — the flag data/dialogue.json ALREADY reads and which, until now, nothing wrote. The other three publish the same shape: `event.migration.<lineId>.open`, `event.bloom.<nodeId>.open`, `event.raid.<raidId>.open`.

encounter._source: build-doc §7.2 derivations — weight = live population count, migrants filtered by season, Scavenger weight × (1 + recentDeaths/scavengerRecentDeathsDivisor). Rates are build-doc-addition tunables.
encounter._throughput: build-doc §4: 'A foray step rolls encounters' (plural) and §3 L8 charges a foray ONE tick — so a foray is an excursion of stepsPerForay steps. A step rolls only on an ENCOUNTER TILE. In the running game that is spatial — the node's EncounterMask says whether the cell the player just stepped onto is grass, and the step rolls at encounterChancePerStep there and at nothing anywhere else. The budget below cannot ask cell by cell, so it uses the position-blind form encounterTileFraction x encounterChancePerStep; see _encounterTileFraction for why the two agree over a route. The player's encounter budget per year is therefore NOT ticksPerYear x stepsPerForay x chance — battles cost clock.battleTicks each, so they consume the same meter the forays do. The honest form is: e = stepsPerForay x encounterTileFraction x encounterChancePerStep encounters per foray, costing forayTicks + e x battleTicks ticks, hence ticksPerYear / (forayTicks + e x battleTicks) forays a year. The year-1 over-catch beat (build-doc §1, §15 I2) is only reachable if that budget beats the target populations' regrowth. Gated by tests/unit/transcription.test.ts.
encounter._encounterTileFraction: THE POSITION-BLIND AVERAGE, and no longer the spatial gate. Until the encounter mask landed this key WAS grass gating: every walked step anywhere on a node rolled at encounterTileFraction x encounterChancePerStep, so a step on a road, in a town square or on a building's doorstep met animals at the rate of a step in tall grass. Where the player stands is now a fact read off the node's EncounterMask (core/foodweb.ts, derived from tools/mapgen/layouts/<id>.txt), so a positioned roll needs no fraction — it is encounterChancePerStep on encounter terrain and nothing anywhere else. This survives for the two callers with no position to read: the year's encounter budget in tests/unit/transcription.test.ts, and tools/harness/full-run.ts, which walks a headless region. For them the honest rate is (share of encounter terrain) x encounterChancePerStep and this is that share as one number. IT IS THE ROUTE SHARE, NOT THE REGION'S: measured over the twelve committed layouts the five routes run 24.10/24.67/25.27/25.16/25.99 % of walkable cells and pool to 24.96 %, which is what 0.25 is; towns run 5.46-10.16 %, the Sanctum 31.02 %, and the whole region pools to 18.63 %. A foray is an excursion into the wild and this budget is a claim about walking routes, so the route band is the right one. Pinned to it by tests/unit/encounter-mask.test.ts so it cannot drift from the maps in silence — which is what stops it being a second opinion about where the grass is (G3). The mask is the only authority on that.
encounter._encounterTerrainChar: The ONE layout character that is encounter terrain: tools/mapgen/legend.ts's `scrub` row, 'walkable but textured — long grass, ferns, heather'. It is here rather than a literal in code for the reason signChainGatedHabitatTag is (G11) — which terrain produces animals is a gameplay decision — and because core/ may not reach tools/mapgen/legend.ts to ask the art lane (tests/gates/guardrails.test.ts no_phaser_in_core holds core/ to data/ and zod). The two lanes are BOUND rather than trusted: tests/gates/layout-encounter-contract.test.ts asserts this character is exactly the legend's scrub row and that it is walkable, so re-lettering the legend reddens instead of silently moving what the game counts as grass.
encounter._finaleGatedNode: bible §8's finale is a SCRIPTED meeting in the Sanctum ring (game/finale.ts), not a foray roll. `maren.keystone.6` writes `chain.vellsire.complete` at act 6 requiring nothing of Greaves, and OverworldScene.unlockedSignChains() unlocks the `hidden` habitat tag on it — so before this key a player could complete the chain, walk into the Sanctum, forage, roll the stag and snare it BEFORE the approach cutscene had played, after which the cutscene narrated an animal the survey said was gone. Sign-chain unlocks are held at this node until `acts.runCompleteFlag` is set. The FLAG is deliberately not repeated here: acts.runCompleteFlag already spells it and core/acts.ts runCompleteFlag() is its reader, so a second spelling would be the two-authorities defect on the flag the whole finale hangs off. kilnback-line (cindershelf) and undermere-line (r2) are unaffected and stay wild.
encounter._levelByYear: BOUND TO THE GYM RAMP in data/gyms.json (8/14/20/26/32/38): the same smooth +6 ramp held exactly two levels under the leader each entry feeds, and asserted against it in tests/unit/transcription.test.ts — at FOUR levels under, the harness's untrained player (the one who only catches and walks in) won gym 1 in 0.2% of 500 seeds. Retuning this key moves the UNTRAINED gym rates only: the TRAINED harness model reads gyms.json and never this array.
encounter._levelByYearIsAnActLadder: THE KEY NAME IS HISTORY; BOTH READERS INDEX IT BY ACT. tools/harness/player.ts has always read it by the LEADER'S act, and these six values are tuned against the gym ramp, which is an act ladder. game/encounters.ts `rollLevel` read it by the CALENDAR YEAR until 2026-08-25, which under an unbounded decoupled calendar meant a player still in act 1 on Route 1 in calendar year 6 met level 34-38 wild creatures against heirs entering at ~5 — a soft fail state by the back door, and the exact pressure Q3 removed. It reads the ACT now, so the two readings agree and the array means one thing. The KEY is not renamed because that is data + core/types.ts + core/schemas.ts + tools/harness, all outside the change that found it; this note is the name.

retirement._source: build-doc §7.5 step 3 — HEIR (level = floor(parent×0.5), inherits 1–2 traits) or BOON (+10% to one stat).
retirement._boonMagnitude: The BOON's +10% is stats.boonModPct and lives ONLY there. A `retirement.boonStatPct` duplicate existed until integration and was deleted per this file's own _singleSource rule: core/battle.ts read stats.boonModPct while core/lifecycle.ts read retirement.boonStatPct, so retuning either alone made the creature card and the battle disagree.
retirement._heirLevelMin: build-doc §7.5 step 3: HEIR level = floor(parentLevel × heirLevelFactor), which gives 0 for a level-1 parent. bible §2 states 'Levels 1–40', so the minimum is 1. encounter.minLevel is NOT reusable here — that is the floor on WILD encounter levels (2), a different rule.
retirement._boonMaxStacks: build-doc §7.5 step 3 gives the BOON a size (+10% to one stat) but no count, so nothing bounded it: a full party of six Elders retiring on the same turn — which is exactly what happens to a party caught together in year 1 — could put six boons on one survivor for +60% to a single stat, and the save validated. The unit of the rule is the bible §2 trait modifier (±10%) and the trait system's own ceiling is traits.maxSlots = 2, so 2 is the matching ceiling here: any one stat can be lifted by at most +20% from legacies.

yearEvents._source: build-doc §7.5 step 5: 'node sims run their 4th season step + year events (Cullbrand raid scripts decrement scripted node populations)'. bible §9 'Cullbrand Harvest raids (scripted per act, populations visibly drop at a named node)'. The raids are DATA, never code: the game only applies whatever this list says. G6 note — a raid may only decrement the harvested populations; it must never touch the predators above them. The predator collapse that makes Cindershelf's arrival read as 'mid-collapse' has to EMERGE from the build-doc §7.3 rules once the prey are gone, which is exactly why the numbers below stop at the two Grazer lines.
yearEvents._actKeyed: RE-KEYED FROM `year` TO `act`. bible §9 always said 'scripted per ACT'; the field said year because content-bible §6 equated the two. A raid now fires on ENTRY to its act, so Cindershelf is entered mid-collapse whether the player arrives in calendar year 2 or year 11. The group keeps the name `yearEvents` because build-doc §7.5 step 5 names it that.
yearEvents._standingStock: A STRIP-HARVEST TAKES THE STANDING STOCK, NOT A FIXED BODY COUNT. Re-keying the raid to the act (`_actKeyed`) made it fire whenever the player earns the act — but the per-target `remove` figures below were authored against r4's SHIPPED counts, and a locked node still breeds every season while the player is elsewhere. Measured through core/ecosim.ts on the shipped r4: arriving at act 4 in calendar year 1 the raid leaves the Grazer tier at 5 of 24 and the Apex reaches 0 in 39 of 64 seeds; arriving in year 4 (the harness's one-act-per-year pacing) the same script leaves 14 of 33 standing and the Apex reaches 0 in 1 of 64; by year 7 the node is at carrying capacity and the Apex never goes at all. So the act-keyed raid did NOT make bible §6's 'arrival mid-collapse' true at every arrival — it made it true at exactly one. `harvestFractionOfStanding` is what fixes that: the harvest is `max(target.remove, round(count × fraction))`, so the authored body count is the floor of the harvest and the fraction carries it at any standing stock. THE NUMBER IS READ OUT OF THE AUTHORED SCRIPT, NOT CHOSEN (G2): the shipped raid removes 11 of 14 Ashvole (0.786) and 8 of 10 Cragmar (0.800), and 0.8 reproduces BOTH authored removes exactly at the shipped state — round(0.8×14)=11, round(0.8×10)=8 — so nothing about the beat as authored moves. G6 is untouched: the fraction scales only what the script harvests, and the collapse above it still has to emerge from the §7.3 rules.

raids._source: bible §6 act 4, Cindershelf: 'arrival mid-collapse — Route 4's web already crashed by Cullbrand strip-harvest'. This is the only raid the bible pins to a named node and act, and THE LIST IS CLOSED AT ONE (T-9, Hank: "Close the raid list at one."). Do not author more. Widening it at this same harvestFractionOfStanding was measured to exterminate lines at the two starter routes, and the shipped dialogue already treats the Cullbrand contract as finished. A per-act raid tier is a proposal for Hank, never an agent edit.

overlayDiff._source: build-doc §8.2 / §9.5 — IoU ≥ 0.85 on dilated Sobel edges within walkable cells; denoise 0.35 stepping −0.05 to a 0.2 floor; ≤3 regen attempts.
overlayDiff._driftFootprintCells: build-doc §8.2 criterion (2) — the largest walkable-mask drift a year variant may carry, in collision cells. It used to be DERIVED in tools/overlay-diff/config.ts as ceil(map.playerSpriteW / map.collisionCellPx) × ceil(map.playerSpriteH / map.collisionCellPx), which put the §9.5 acceptance criterion out of INV-3's reach: loosening it after a supervised run meant editing code. Shipped at the derived value (2 × 3) so this is a no-op move; a retune raises it here alone. The floor is the player's own footprint — a tolerance smaller than the player admits a drift that can strand him — and tests/unit/balance-inv3.test.ts holds it there.

map._source: build-doc §7.6 — virtual 480×320 integer-scaled; painted maps 1024² rendered 2×; mask sampled on a 16px grid (64×64 cells); player 32×48, tile step 32.
map._spriteTargets: build-doc §9.3 — 'nearest-neighbor downscale to target (battle 96², overworld chars 32×48, minis 32²)'. The overworld size has been playerSpriteW/H all along; the other two were literals in game/ui/BattleLayout.ts and pins in tools/comfy/manifest.json. Both are square, so one number each.
map._walkMsPerTile: PRESENTATION pace, not a simulation number: a foray is counted in STEPS (balance.encounter.stepsPerForay), so a faster walk costs exactly the same ticks and moves no population. It is here because it was a literal in game/movement.ts and INV-3 says a retune touches this file only. 160ms/tile is four tiles a second at the §7.6 virtual resolution.
map._skip: THE PLAYER ALWAYS FACES THE VIEWER AND SKIPS (Hank's ruling: 'we're switching to the player character always being facing forward and doing the skipping movement as it moves around'). The motion is build-doc §9.6 step 4's bob, which has THREE terms and is quoted verbatim: 'y = 2px sine per tile step, 1px lateral sway, horizontal flip alternation'. The flip is the load-bearing one — a pure vertical sine on a static sprite reads as a FLOAT, and mirroring on alternate hops is what makes the eye read a change of weight instead. All of it is PRESENTATION ONLY: game/movement.ts's skipOffsetPx / skipSwayOffsetPx / skipFlipped are read by OverworldScene.syncPlayerSprite and by nothing else, so retuning any of them cannot move the player one pixel as far as collision, the logical tile or propUnderPlayer are concerned. Retune here and nowhere else (INV-3).
map._skipHopPx: Peak height of one hop above the resting draw position. §9.6 step 4 says '2px' and this is that number, in WORLD pixels — RECONCILED, because the two are the same here and the arithmetic is worth writing down: mapRenderScale 2× is a property of the painted MAP (1024² native shown at 2048²) and NOT of characters. The player is authored at playerSpriteW×playerSpriteH (32×48, build-doc §9.3 'overworld chars 32×48', manifest classes.player.targetW/H) and drawn at exactly that size by OverworldScene's setDisplaySize, so one sprite pixel is one world pixel is one screen pixel at the §7.6 virtual resolution. 2 sprite px is therefore 2 world px, not 4. The schema floor is 1 because a hop of zero is a reversal of the ruling, not a retune.
map._skipSwayPx: §9.6 step 4's '1px lateral sway' — the screen-x half of the bob, at its widest, in the same world pixels as skipHopPx. It leans the way the sprite is mirrored, so the sway and the flip are one gesture rather than two; on the same sine envelope as the hop, so it starts and ends the tile step at zero and consecutive steps chain instead of snapping.
map._skipHopsPerTile: How many hops one tile step is spent on, and therefore how often the sprite mirrors. §9.6 says 'per tile step', i.e. 1: at walkMsPerTile 160 that is 6.25 hops a second, which reads as a skip; 2 would be 12.5 and reads as a vibration. Also the divisor of the arc's phase, so a whole number is the only value that lands the sprite back on the ground exactly at the tile boundary.

party._source: build-doc §3 L12 / §7.8 — versioned JSON in localStorage, 3 slots.
party._saveVersion: BUMPED 1 → 2 with the two-clock change. core/acts.ts `story.actEntered` is the latch that says which acts a save has already ENTERED, and a save written before it exists has no latch — so `lastActEntered` reads `first - 1` and the game re-enters acts 0..N on the first frame, re-applying the act-4 Cullbrand raid ON TOP of the harvest the old build already applied. Measured on a mid-run v1 save (3 badges, r4 already harvested once): ashvole 3 → 0, cragmar 2 → 0, recentDeaths 19 → 24, i.e. an extinction the player did not cause, which then feeds the derived cascade. A new save is indistinguishable from an old one by questFlags alone (both have no latch), so the VERSION is the only thing that can tell them apart. core/save.ts `deserialize` refuses a v1 save with the documented message; saves are not migrated (demo scope).

economy._source: bible §11 — snares ×3 tiers, baits role-generic vs species-specific, medicines, inn rest. Prices are build-doc-addition tunables; medicine EFFECTS are in `medicine`.
economy._innCost: NOT one of the flat prices below, deliberately. Hank's ruling: 'innCost is already paid through ticks' — a rest costs `clock.innTicks`, and this coin figure is the second half of a price that is mostly time. It was 40 before the flat-price pass and it is 40 after it. Do not 'correct' it to match the others.
economy._prices: EVERY PURCHASABLE PRICE IS 3, AND THIS IS WHERE 3 CAME FROM. Hank ruled twice and the SECOND ruling is the one this number obeys. First: 'the other prices can all be the same, just for simplicity... base it off the estimated amount of money that a player can expect to earn over the course of an in-game year... a player should be able to buy 40 of those items total in a year.' That was implemented as 25, from the SIX-ACT MEAN income of 996 a year (996/40 = 24.9). Shown that 25 buys about five items in act 1 against eighty-six in act 6, he amended it: 'Make it so that the expected earnings in year one specifically can buy 40.' THE ANCHOR IS YEAR ONE, NOT THE MEAN. The only earner the shipped game has is a won rival fight (core/save.ts trainerPayout, at trainerPayoutPerLevel below). The ACT-1 rival, Wick at r1, fields a level-6 slot plus a level-6 Carricrow signature: 12 x (6+6) = 144. 144 / 40 items = 3.6. WHY 3 AND NOT 3.6: money is an INTEGER quantity on the tape. core/save.ts readPayout and applyPayout BOTH refuse a fractional amount outright, throwing SaveCorruptError, because a fraction the live path accepts and the replay arm declines to rebuild is locked decision L10 going silently false - the exact shape in which {t:innRest} once shipped with no replay arm at all. A fractional price would need a rounding rule at the till; no such rule exists and none was ruled on. Of the two integers either side: 4 buys 36 in year one and MISSES the target, 3 buys 48 and MEETS it with margin. Hence 3. THE CONSEQUENCE A LATER READER MUST NOT LOSE, because it is large and it was accepted knowingly: income is still not uniform. Act 1 pays 144 and act 6 pays 2160, so at 3 apiece act 1 affords 48 items and act 6 affords 720 - about 1,992 across the whole run, against the 240 the original phrasing described. Money is tight ONLY in year one and is effectively unlimited from act 3 on. That is the shape of anchoring a flat price to the poorest year, and no flat price avoids it: the price buying exactly 40 in each act runs 3.6, 10.8, 16.2, 28.8, 36 and 54, a fifteen-fold spread. Forty in EVERY act is a different rule needing an act-indexed price or a change to the purses.
economy._baitPrice: `none` is 0 because 'no bait' is an option a player always has, not a bait that happens to be free — it is the identity row of `catch.baitMult`, and it is left at 0 by the flat-price pass on purpose. Measured before touching it: `grep -rn 'baitPrice' core game tools tests data` returns only this file, `core/types.ts` and `core/schemas.ts` — nothing reads `none` as a price, or reads any of these prices at all yet.
economy._trainerPayout: A PURSE IS A FLAT FEE PLUS A PER-LEVEL RATE, and the flat half exists to bend the curve. Hank's ruling: 'Make it so that earnings don't scale quite as much. I think it's a hallmark of Pokemon games that you eventually have way too much money at some point, but that point shouldn't be until probably Act 5.' A purely per-level purse could not do that: the rival's roster grows from two level-6 creatures to five level-36 ones, so the summed levels run 12, 36, 54, 96, 120, 180 and ANY flat rate reproduces that same 15x spread. Money was therefore already abundant by act 2. Adding a flat per-fight component compresses the ratio without touching one line of content (G2): payout = trainerPayoutFlat + trainerPayoutPerLevel x sum(levels). At 100 + 3x the purses become 136, 208, 262, 388, 460, 640 - a 4.7x spread instead of 15x. Measured against what a year actually costs (~47 weighted snares for the r4 cascade beat plus ~27 to fill a party = ~74 items at 3 apiece), the player can afford 0.6x, 0.9x, 1.2x, 1.7x, 2.1x and 2.9x of a year's need across the six acts - genuinely short in acts 1-2, comfortable at act 5, rich at act 6, which is the shape the ruling asks for. Act 1 still clears the earlier ruling that year one buys forty items: 136/3 = 45. AN EMPTY ROSTER PAYS NOTHING, and that is a guard rather than arithmetic - without it the flat fee would pay out for a fight against no one.
economy._gates: TWO CONTENT IDS THE ECONOMY GATES ON, here rather than in code. Hank's ruling: 'Weighted Snares unlocked in the shop after the second gym is completed... the player be given three master snares at the completion of the fifth gym.' `weightedUnlockGym` is the SECOND leader and `masterSnareGrant` is his three. Both lived briefly as literals in game/ - `game/shop.ts` WEIGHTED_UNLOCK_GYM and a cast in OverworldScene - because zod STRIPS keys the schema does not declare (core/acts.ts records this as INV-3), so adding a key to this file alone reaches no reader and the move needed this file, core/types.ts and core/schemas.ts together. Note what stays derived: the badge FLAG is never written down. core/acts.ts badgeFlagFor builds it from acts.badgeFlagPrefix + the gym id + acts.badgeFlagSuffix, the one grammar the game reads badges through, so retuning the prefix moves this gate with it. ⚠ THE GYM ID IS NOT CROSS-VALIDATED against data/gyms.json - the schema only checks it is a non-empty string, so a typo here would silently never unlock the shelf rather than failing at boot. game/shop.ts refuses loudly instead; if that ever changes, this is the hole.

audio._source: bible §12a procedural treatments — season DSP presets and progressive year darkening.

_seasonTint: Hard Requirement 6 — 'Season variation is a runtime tint shader; year variation is art. Never generate seasonal map art.' The four hues are the tint game/season-tint.ts multiplies over whichever painted map is on screen. The MAGNITUDES that dim them (audio.seasonBrightness, audio.yearDarkenPerYear) are their own keys above; these are the HUES, and they were literals in game/season-tint.ts until 2026-08-26. A channel is 0–255 and 255 means 'leave this channel alone' — setTint multiplies — so the reading normalises each preset to peak 255 before the two magnitudes are applied (see hueOf). overlayAlpha is the strength of the optional full-screen overlay pass a scene may draw above the tinted map. One preset per season, exhaustively: the group is a z.record over the Season enum, which unlike every other group here REJECTS an unrecognised key rather than stripping it — hence this note living outside the group.

harness._source: build-doc §10.5 — gym win-rate targets 80–95 / 60–80 / 45–65 by pair, round-robin flags outside 35–65%, 500 seeds.

overcatch._source: build-doc §1 demo beat 1 (never-cut) + §15 I2: 'cascade demo reproducible from overcatch-script.json in real play'. This group states the reference player the feasibility gate assumes — a determined player working ONE walkable node, using the snare tier and bait below and throwing at referenceHpFrac. The gate (tests/unit/transcription.test.ts) requires that this player can drive an Apex's derived prey pool under the starvation threshold within yearsBudget years DESPITE regrowth.

perf._source: build-doc §12 — ecosim.step all 12 nodes < 5ms with ×4 margin on mega-node; battle reducer < 1ms/action; save serialize < 50ms; boot < 3s.

rng._source: build-doc §8.1 — one seeded xorshift128 stream per subsystem, seeds derived from save seed + subsystem tag. the seeded stream is the only source of randomness in the project (G11).
rng._subsystemTags: APPEND-ONLY, and the order is load-bearing: tools/harness/content.ts reads the first three positionally as (battle, sim, encounter). 'lifecycle' was added on 2026-08-26 — core/lifecycle.ts's heir roll draws randomness and had no stream of its own, so game/scenes/OverworldScene.ts composed its key out of the SIM tag. Each tag is seeded independently (hashSeed(saveSeed + tag)), so adding one moves no other stream by a single draw.
